dailyRead: Yesterday this page carried two downgrades built on a single premise - that the Middle East risk premium was deflating fast enough to break the monetary case under AUD and CAD - and in the twenty-four hours since, that premise has been contradicted on the tape and the dollar story has become something larger than a rates story. Take the dollar first, because it is now the board. S&P Global's September flash survey put US manufacturing at 57.0 against a 53.6 forecast and 53.9 in August, services at 58.7 from 56.5, and the composite at 58.4 from 56.0 - TradingEconomics carries all three - and the press release adds the two lines that matter more than the headline: the surveys' price gauges rose to their highest since October 2022 and employment growth ran at a pace not seen since mid-2022. Fed Governor Michael Barr then told a Chicago housing conference that in his base case 'further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion', and that risks to the inflation target have increased while risks to the labour market have receded; Austan Goolsbee said in the same session that 'this has been nothing like the one-and-done pattern that underpins the case for looking through.' CME FedWatch odds for October 28 went to about 73%, from the 59.7% this page verified yesterday and roughly 55% on Tuesday, and TradingEconomics reported the US 10-year closing at 5.04%, the highest since July 2007, with its bond board carrying 5.117% this morning. DXY at 101.083 is a two-month high, +0.83% on the week and +2.19% on the month. That is a dollar bid on growth and on term premium at once, and it is why every USD pair on this board points the same way. The single crack worth naming is the US consumer: September confidence fell to 47.8 from 51.7, within four points of its all-time low, which is what a 108% year-on-year gasoline price does to a household even while businesses report the best conditions in four years. Now the correction this page owes itself. Yesterday AUD was cut from +1 to 0, on a labour force survey that was soft beneath a strong headline and on the pre-committed trigger that crude extending lower would do it. The jobs read was right on the detail - full-time employment fell 6,300, unemployment rose to 4.6%, a five-year high, with the whole gain part-time - but the conclusion was wrong on the evidence that actually prices the RBA. Market pricing did not move on the print: it sits at about 95% for a hike to 4.60% on September 29, all four Australian majors now forecast that hike, and the crude leg of the downgrade reversed outright, with WTI back to 91.404 from 89.263 and Brent back over 100 at 102.166. AUD returns to +1 and the specific fact that changed is the pricing, not a new data point. Note carefully that TradingEconomics has now put an explicit TEForecast of 4.35% on the September 29 row - a dated hold where yesterday it carried only a quarter-end level - so the disagreement between the canonical source and the market is sharper today than it has ever been on this page, and it resolves in five days. Europe is the other upgrade. The euro-area flash composite rose to 53.1 from 52.0 against a 51.5 consensus, the fastest in almost three and a half years, with services at 53.0 against 51.7 expected and Germany's composite at 53.8 against 51.8; the Bund 10-year is back above 3.5% at 3.5495, the highest since mid-2009; and the ECB's own calendar, read at ecb.europa.eu, dates the next decision to October 29 with a press conference - something TradingEconomics' calendar still does not carry. With HICP at 3.2% and rising, Nagel already having said out loud he cannot exclude mildly restrictive territory, and a deposit rate of 2.50%, EUR goes to +1. Sterling is the mirror image and yesterday's downgrade holds: the UK composite fell to 51.7 from 52.5 with services missing at 51.7 against 52.0 expected, the only major economy whose September survey went the wrong way, and the gilt 10-year at 5.348% is the highest yield on this board for the wrong reason, five weeks before a Budget that August borrowing of 18.3 billion already made harder. Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow is the event. The yen is unchanged at 0 and is being held in place by two opposite forces that both got stronger: US yields at 19-year highs dragged USD/JPY to 158.283 yesterday, and the Ministry of Finance's August coordinated operation with the US Treasury plus last Friday's reported rate check sit directly above; spot is 157.904 and -0.27% on the day, which is a market that has noticed. Canada stays at -1, and the reason is worth stating precisely now that crude has bounced: Canada's problem has stopped being only its terms of trade. Employment fell 41,700 in August, the services PMI at 46.8 and the composite at 47.8 are the only contracting activity readings on this board, and the July retail sales print at 12:30Z today is the test. Switzerland decides at 07:30Z. Every source carries 0.00%, so the assessment is about the conditional inflation path - Swiss CPI has doubled to 0.8% from 0.4% on energy - and about whether the intervention clause stays in its 'increased willingness' form now that the franc has weakened 2.84% against the dollar on the month rather than strengthened. The cleanest expressions of all of this are USD/CAD and DXY long, EUR/GBP long, AUD/NZD long, and the metals short that the real-rate move now justifies on both gold and silver.

HICP 3.2% and rising with core 2.4%, PPI 5.8%, GDP +1.2% y/y from +0.6%, unemployment 6.4%, wage growth 3.0%. Bund 10-year 3.5495, highest since mid-2009. EUR/USD 1.13840, -0.80% week, -2.49% month.
strength.forward: 🦅 Leaning hawkish into October 29, a date verified on the ECB's own Governing Council calendar and not yet carried by TE. Nagel said on September 22 he cannot exclude the ECB needing to turn mildly restrictive and that rates are still in neutral territory; the September survey gives that view a growth number to stand on, and TE's model path of 3.15 percent in 2027 points the same way. Invalidation is the October flash survey giving back the September jump, or HICP rolling over from 3.2% - the euro is still losing to the dollar on the week despite all of this, so this is a cross-based upgrade, not a EUR/USD call.

strength.tag: Upgraded back: pricing did not move, and crude did
strength.drivers: Cash rate 4.35%, the highest on this board, with market pricing about 95% for a hike to 4.60% on September 29 and all four Australian majors now forecasting it - unmoved by the August labour force survey. That survey: employment +39,493 against a 21.5K forecast, but full-time -6,282, part-time +45,775, unemployment 4.6% (a five-year high) against a 4.5% forecast, participation 67.10% from 66.90%. Core CPI 3.6% with headline 3.5%, above the 2-3% band. September flash PMIs: manufacturing 49.3 from 52.0, services 51.4 from 53.2, composite 50.8 from 52.7. GDP 2.1% y/y, wage growth 3.2%. AUD/USD 0.70348, -1.07% week. Copper 6.6942, +1.64% week; WTI back to 91.404.
strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish into September 29, with the verdict left at MIXED because the domestic activity data genuinely contradicts the policy call. Bullock has retired the narrow-path framing and says heat needs to come out of the labour market; the supply shock she is hiking into is live again with Brent back over 100. TE has now attached an explicit 4.35% TEForecast to the meeting, so this is the sharpest canonical-versus-market disagreement on the board. Invalidation is concrete and dated: a hold on September 29 takes this straight back to 0, and the 95% pricing means the asymmetry on a hold is violent. A hike with a dovish statement is the second-order risk.

strength.tag: Steepest projected path, second weakest economy
strength.drivers: Official cash rate 2.75%, raised from 2.50% on September 2, a second consecutive hike, with TE carrying 2.75% unchanged at October 28 and a TEForecast of 3.0% at December 9; reporting puts market pricing for an October hike at roughly 75%. CPI 4.1%, the highest on this board, with core 3.2%. Against that: unemployment 5.6% and rising from 5.4%, Q2 GDP +0.2% q/q from +0.9% though the annual rate rose to 2.6% from 1.7%, wage growth 2.1%, retail sales -0.5% m/m, manufacturing PMI 53.1 and services 51.2. NZ 10-year 5.081. NZD/USD 0.56746, -0.98% week and -5.06% month, the worst monthly of the eight.
strength.forward: 🦅 Hawkish path, weak carrier. TE's model at 4.00 percent in 2027 is 125bp above spot, the steepest projected tightening anywhere here, and Governor Breman's warning that persistent oil increases could push near-term inflation above forecast has pulled market pricing onto October. Invalidation runs both ways: a confirmed October hike upgrades this to +1, while a Q3 labour report pushing unemployment through 5.8% or a retreat in oil would leave the OCR track looking like a forecast the economy cannot carry.

strength.tag: Decision day, and the rate is not the event
strength.drivers: SNB policy rate 0.00%, held in March and June, with TE's TEForecast, the ForexFactory consensus and the Reuters economist poll all carrying 0% for 07:30Z today. CPI has doubled to 0.8% in August from 0.4%, core 0.4%, producer prices -0.7%. The cyclical data is the strongest set on this board: GDP +2.3% y/y from +0.4%, manufacturing PMI 57.1 from 53.2, services 58.3, unemployment 3.0%, employment +0.5%. Swiss 10-year 0.570, the lowest here by a distance. USD/CHF 0.82421, franc 2.84% weaker on the month; EUR/CHF implied near 0.9383.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Range, pending the words at 08:00Z. Two live variables: whether the conditional inflation path published in June at 0.6%/0.6%/0.7% is marked up on energy pass-through, and whether the 'increased willingness to intervene' clause survives now that the franc is weakening rather than appreciating. A markup plus retained hawkish FX language is franc-positive; a reversion to symmetric standby wording reads as the SNB stepping back and is the franc-negative outcome. Invalidation of the neutral stance is either of those arriving clearly - which is why the franc crosses are held at RANGE into the event rather than positioned.

strength.tag: Carry pulling one way, the MoF standing the other
strength.drivers: Policy rate 1.25%, raised from 1.00% on September 18 in a 7-2 vote, the highest since April 1995, with TE carrying a TEForecast of 1.25% at October 30 - an explicit hold - and its model at 1.75 percent in 2027. CPI 1.9% with core easing to 1.7% from 1.8%; BoJ core CPI prints 05:00Z tomorrow at a 1.5% forecast. Wage growth 4.7%, accelerating from 4.0%. Unemployment 2.4%. September flash PMIs softened throughout: manufacturing 54.1 from 54.9, services 51.6 from 52.5, composite 52.5 from 53.5. JGB 10-year 3.083, +1.43 points in twelve months. USD/JPY 157.904 after touching 158.283, -0.27% on the day and +1.24% on the week.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Balanced and event-driven. The yen is short the largest yield gap in this cycle and long the most credible intervention threat on the board: Japan and the US ran a coordinated operation in August and said they would not hesitate to repeat it, Katayama has stressed continuing communication with the US Treasury, and a rate check was reported late Friday into holiday liquidity. Invalidation of the neutral call is either a confirmed intervention, which takes the yen sharply higher and this score positive, or a clean break above 158.30 that goes unanswered, which would say the threat has been tested and found empty.

strength.tag: Loses the growth comparison on both sides
strength.drivers: Bank Rate 3.75%, held September 17 with Vote Hike 3/9 and Vote Cut 0/9. September flash PMIs went the wrong way and were the only ones on this board to do so: composite 51.7 from 52.5, services 51.7 against a 52.0 expectation, manufacturing 52.0 from 51.7. CPI 3.1% and rising with core 2.6% and PPI 3.7%. Wage growth cooling to 3.9% from 4.2%, unemployment 4.9%, employment change +67K from +83K, claimant count +27.8K. August public sector net borrowing 18.3 billion against 15.7 billion expected, the financial year to August 8.1 billion above the OBR forecast, Budget October 28. Gilt 10-year 5.348, the highest yield here. GBP/USD 1.32407, a twelve-week low.
strength.forward: ⚖️ Range with a hawkish tail. TE's calendar still lists a December 17 Vote Hike row and a Vote Unchanged row and NO Vote Cut row, and its model projects 4.00 percent in 2027, so the canonical path carries a move up before it carries one down - but the survey round just took away the growth argument for it. Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow is the decisive input: explicit tolerance of above-target inflation into the Budget is the upgrade, an acknowledgement that the September survey softening changes the November calculus is the downgrade. Three MPC speakers today are the warm-up.

strength.tag: Crude repaired the conditional, not the economy
strength.drivers: Policy rate 2.25%, held on September 2, which TE carries flat through 2027 and lower only in 2028 - the widest policy gap on this board against a Fed at 4.00%. August employment -41,700 with full-time -35,900; services PMI 46.8 and composite 47.8, the only contracting activity readings here; retail sales carried at -0.8% m/m for July with core -0.5% and the official print at 12:30Z today. CPI 3.0% with core 2.4%, producer prices 12.4%, unemployment 6.4%, wage growth 3.4%, GDP +1.1% y/y. Canada 10-year 3.953, the lowest here outside Japan and Switzerland. USD/CAD 1.41048, +0.81% week and +1.93% month.
strength.forward: 🔻 Dovish-by-default into October 28. Macklem's hawkish conditional was written at US$100 oil and Brent at 102.166 has gone back through it, which is the first thing to improve for the loonie in a week and the reason this is -1 rather than -2; reporting has him saying the October meeting will consider whether to raise or hold. Against that, the domestic data gives him nothing to raise into. Invalidation is a retail sales beat today followed by a Business Outlook Survey on October 19 that does not show demand deteriorating - or crude holding above 100 long enough that the inflation the Bank says it can look through stops looking temporary.

symbols.why: Still the widest gap on the board at four points and now supported from the rates side rather than the oil side: a Fed at 4.00% with October hike odds at about 73% and a 10-year that closed at a 19-year high, against a Bank of Canada frozen at 2.25% that TE carries flat into 2027 and a Canada 10-year at 3.953%. Canada's services PMI at 46.8 and composite at 47.8 are the only contracting activity readings here and August employment fell 41,700. Spot 1.41048, +0.81% week and +1.93% month.
symbols.risk: The crude leg has reversed on you: Brent back through 100 at 102.166 revives exactly the conditional Macklem wrote, and a further Hormuz escalation would put the loonie's terms of trade back on the right side. July retail sales at 12:30Z today, carried at -0.8% with core -0.5%, is the near-term trigger and a clear beat argues for taking the trade down rather than adding.

symbols.why: The index is 101.083 at a two-month high, +0.83% on the week and +2.19% on the month, and the driver broadened overnight from policy to growth: a composite PMI of 58.4, the strongest since July 2021, price gauges at a four-year high, October hike odds at about 73% and a 10-year closing at 5.04%. The weights help - EUR 57.6% is strengthening but still -0.80% on the week against the dollar, JPY 13.6% is capped by carry, GBP 11.9% is the weakest survey on the board and CAD 9.1% is the weakest currency here.
symbols.risk: It is long a great deal of good news. US consumer confidence collapsed to 47.8 from 51.7, within four points of its all-time low, and claims at 12:30Z today plus four Fed speakers are the first places that can go the other way. The 57.6% euro weight also means today's ifo and any follow-through from the euro-area survey jump works directly against the index.

symbols.why: The cleanest relative-growth trade of the survey round. The euro-area composite jumped to 53.1 from 52.0 against a 51.5 consensus with Germany at 53.8 against 51.8, while the UK composite fell to 51.7 from 52.5 with services missing - the only major to move the wrong way. Add a deposit rate rising to 2.50% and a dated ECB meeting on October 29 against a Bank Rate frozen at 3.75% and a Budget on October 28 that August's 18.3 billion borrowing print made harder, and the divergence is real on both legs.
symbols.risk: Sterling has a live hawkish tail: three of nine MPC members voted to hike eight days ago, CPI is 3.1% and rising, and Bailey speaks at 09:15Z tomorrow with Dhingra, Breeden and Lombardelli today. A Bailey message that November is genuinely open would unwind this quickly, and the gilt 10-year at 5.348% means sterling is not short yield.

symbols.why: Flipped up from RANGE on a policy-divergence read that now has dates on both sides. The RBA meets September 29 with market pricing about 95% for a hike to 4.60% and all four Australian majors forecasting it, while TE carries the RBNZ at 2.75% unchanged on October 28 and puts 3.0% only at December 9. Australia's cash rate is already the highest on the board at 4.35% with core CPI at 3.6%; New Zealand carries unemployment at 5.6% and rising, wage growth of 2.1% and Q2 GDP that slowed to +0.2% q/q.
symbols.risk: The RBA hike is 95% priced, so the entire asymmetry is on a hold - and TE's canonical calendar carries exactly that, an explicit 4.35% TEForecast. Reporting also puts an October RBNZ hike at roughly 75% after Governor Breman's oil-inflation warning, which would close the divergence from the other side. Australia's own activity data is contracting at 49.3 manufacturing.

symbols.why: A three-point gap running in the same direction on growth, policy and fiscal at once. The US composite PMI is 58.4 and the UK's is 51.7 and falling; the Fed is at 4.00% with 73% odds of 4.25% on October 28 while the Bank of England is frozen at 3.75%; and the gilt 10-year at 5.348% is high for fiscal reasons five weeks before a Budget. Spot 1.32407 is a twelve-week low, -0.89% on the week and -2.99% on the month.
symbols.risk: Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow is a red folder and the MPC's hawkish minority is real - no member voted to cut on September 17 and three voted to hike. A US claims print above 215K today or a second weak consumer read would take the dollar leg out at the same time.

symbols.why: The weakest currency on the board against the strongest, with a three-point score gap. New Zealand carries unemployment at 5.6% and rising, Q2 GDP slowing to +0.2% q/q, wage growth of 2.1% and an OCR of 2.75% against a Fed at 4.00% heading for 4.25%. Spot 0.56746 is -0.98% on the week and -5.06% on the month, the worst monthly performance of the eight, and it is grinding toward the floor of its range.
symbols.risk: The forward case is the opposite of the spot case: TE's model has the OCR at 4.00 percent in 2027, the steepest projected tightening here, CPI is 4.1% - the highest on this board - and reporting puts an October hike at roughly 75% after Breman's oil-inflation warning. A confirmed October hike would force this to be re-read.

symbols.why: A two-point gap that narrowed today and still points the same way. The euro-area survey jump to 53.1 is genuine and lifts EUR to +1, but it was outrun on the same morning: the US composite printed 58.4 with price gauges at a four-year high, October hike odds moved to about 73%, and the Treasury-Bund 10-year spread widened with the US at 5.117% against 3.5495. Spot 1.13840, -0.80% on the week and -2.49% on the month.
symbols.risk: This is the narrowest of the dollar longs and the one with a live catalyst against it. If Nagel's 'mildly restrictive' language starts appearing from other Council members with the October 29 meeting now dated, the euro leg re-rates quickly. The ifo and the ECB Economic Bulletin at 08:00Z are today's tests, and a US claims miss would hit both legs at once.

symbols.why: A two-point gap between the board's clearest upgrade and its only weakening currency. The euro-area composite at 53.1 is the fastest in three and a half years with a deposit rate rising to 2.50% and a dated October 29 meeting; Canada's composite is 47.8, its services PMI 46.8, employment fell 41,700 in August, and the policy rate is carried flat at 2.25% through 2027. The Bund at 3.5495 against Canada at 3.953 makes the yield pickup small enough not to offset it.
symbols.risk: Brent back above 102 is a direct CAD tailwind and revives Macklem's US$100 conditional, and a retail sales beat at 12:30Z today would give the loonie two pieces of good news in a session. The euro leg is one survey old - an ifo miss at 08:00Z would make the upgrade look premature.

symbols.why: Two commodity currencies separated by their central banks. Australia is at 4.35% with about 95% priced for 4.60% in five days and core CPI at 3.6%; Canada is at 2.25% flat through 2027 with a contracting services sector. The crude rebound helps both, so the differentiator is policy, and it is a two-point gap in Australia's favour. Copper at 6.6942 and +1.64% on the week supports the Australian side of the terms-of-trade read.
symbols.risk: Both legs are exposed to the same thing in opposite directions: crude. Brent through 100 helps Canada more than Australia in the short run, and a September 29 RBA hold - which is TE's own explicit forecast - would remove the entire premise while Canadian retail sales at 12:30Z could beat today.

symbols.why: A two-point gap, but the narrowest conviction of the dollar shorts because the Australian leg is improving into an event. Spot 0.70348 is a seven-week low, -1.07% on the week, driven by the US side: a 58.4 composite PMI, a 19-year-high 10-year and about 73% odds of an October hike. Australia's own activity data is contracting at 49.3 manufacturing and 50.8 composite with unemployment at a five-year high of 4.6%.
symbols.risk: About 95% of an RBA hike to 4.60% is priced for September 29 with all four Australian majors behind it, and a hike delivered with hawkish guidance into a live crude shock would take this back quickly. Crude reversing higher removes the terms-of-trade argument that made this a cleaner short last week.

symbols.why: One point of separation between a euro area whose composite just hit a three-and-a-half-year high with a rising deposit rate, and a New Zealand economy carrying 5.6% unemployment, wage growth of 2.1% and Q2 GDP at +0.2% q/q. The kiwi is the worst monthly performer on the board at -5.06% and Germany's 53.8 composite is the best single-country print here after the US.
symbols.risk: New Zealand has the steepest projected policy path on this board - TE's model at 4.00 percent in 2027 - the highest inflation at 4.1%, and roughly 75% priced for an October hike. If that October move is confirmed while the euro-area survey proves a one-month spike, this inverts.

symbols.why: One point of separation and it rests on Canada rather than on Britain. Canada is the only weakening currency here, with a contracting services PMI at 46.8, employment down 41,700 and a policy rate flat at 2.25% through 2027, while the Bank of England still has three of nine members voting to hike and no member voting to cut, with CPI at 3.1% and rising.
symbols.risk: Both currencies got worse news than expected in the last 24 hours - a UK survey that fell to 51.7 and a crude rebound that helps the loonie - so this is a trade between two impaired legs. Canadian retail sales at 12:30Z and Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow are both live, and the October 28 Budget sits against sterling.

symbols.why: One point of separation between two of the weaker currencies here, and the case is relative policy direction: the RBNZ has hiked twice since July to 2.75% with roughly 75% now priced for a third in October, against a Bank of Canada that TE carries flat at 2.25% through 2027 with the only contracting activity data on this board.
symbols.risk: The lowest-quality long on this page - it pairs the worst monthly performer against the currency whose case improved most overnight. Brent above 102 revives Macklem's conditional directly, and a Canadian retail sales beat at 12:30Z would leave this with nothing behind it.

symbols.why: A three-point score gap and the widest carry of the cycle: a Fed at 4.00% with a 10-year that closed at 5.04%, against a Bank of Japan at 1.25% that TE explicitly forecasts to hold on October 30 and a JGB at 3.083. Japan's September survey softened everywhere and core CPI eased to 1.7%. Spot 157.904 after touching 158.283 yesterday.
symbols.risk: The highest event risk on the board, and the reason conviction stays low despite the widest gap. Japan and the US ran a coordinated intervention in August and said they would not hesitate to repeat it, Katayama has stressed continuing communication with the US Treasury, and a rate check was reported late Friday. Wage growth at 4.7% and TE's 1.75 percent 2027 path both argue the BoJ is not finished.

symbols.why: Three points of separation and a franc already moving the right way - spot 0.82421 with the franc 2.84% weaker on the month - against a Fed at 4.00% heading for a likely 4.25% and a Swiss policy rate TE's model carries at 0.00 percent through 2027, the only flat-at-zero path here. The Swiss 10-year at 0.570 is the lowest on the board by a wide margin.
symbols.risk: The SNB decides at 07:30Z today with the press conference at 08:00Z, so this is a position into a red folder. Swiss CPI doubling to 0.8% argues for a marked-up conditional inflation path, and if the 'increased willingness to intervene' clause is retained in hawkish form the franc rallies against a dollar that is already long a lot of good news.

symbols.why: One point of separation, newly created by the euro-area upgrade. The bloc's composite at 53.1 is the fastest in three and a half years with a deposit rate at 2.50% and a dated October 29 meeting, against a Bank of Japan TE explicitly forecasts to hold at 1.25% on October 30 with core CPI easing to 1.7% and every September survey component softer. The Bund at 3.5495 against the JGB at 3.083 supports the carry.
symbols.risk: Yen-cross longs are all the same trade against the same tail: a confirmed Ministry of Finance intervention would take every one of them down at once, and USD/JPY at 158.283 yesterday sat in the zone where the August operation was run. Japanese wage growth at 4.7% also argues the BoJ hold is not permanent.

symbols.why: One point of separation, and the cleanest expression of the AUD upgrade on a cross without dollar interference. The RBA is 95% priced to take the cash rate to 4.60% in five days against a Bank of Japan TE forecasts to hold at 1.25%, giving the widest developed-market carry after USD/JPY, and the crude rebound that revived the RBA's supply-shock case is a direct yen negative as an energy importer.
symbols.risk: Two-sided on both legs. A September 29 RBA hold - TE's own explicit forecast - removes the Australian case, while an MoF intervention removes the yen case, and the pair would take both hits in the same direction. Australia's contracting manufacturing survey at 49.3 remains the domestic argument against.

symbols.why: One point of separation on the Australian upgrade, expressed against the lowest policy rate on the board. Australia's 4.35% heading for a likely 4.60% against a Swiss 0.00% that TE carries flat through 2027 is the widest absolute rate gap available here, and the franc is weakening rather than bid, with USD/CHF up 2.84% on the month.
symbols.risk: Both sides carry a dated event within five days: the SNB at 07:30Z today, where hawkish FX language would bid the franc, and the RBA on September 29, where TE's own forecast is a hold against 95% market pricing for a hike. Holding this into both is the definition of low conviction.

symbols.why: One point of separation on the euro-area upgrade, and the single most SNB-sensitive pair on this board. A deposit rate at 2.50% and a composite PMI at 53.1 against a policy rate at zero is the fundamental case; the implied cross near 0.9383 reflects a franc that has been weakening rather than appreciating.
symbols.risk: Conviction is deliberately the lowest here because the decision is ninety minutes away. The June assessment's 'increased willingness to intervene' clause was written to counter rapid franc APPRECIATION, which is not the current problem; a reversion to symmetric standby wording is euro-positive, but a marked-up conditional inflation path with the hawkish clause retained would move this cross several figures the other way.

symbols.why: One point of separation, shorting the board's only weakening currency against a yen with an intervention bid beneath it. Canada's services PMI is 46.8 with employment down 41,700 and a policy rate flat at 2.25% through 2027; Japan has wage growth at 4.7%, a policy rate that has risen to 1.25% and a JGB 10-year at 3.083.
symbols.risk: This is now a fight against the crude rebound. Brent through 102 supports the loonie directly and Canada's rate still sits a full point above Japan's, so the carry runs against the position. A Canadian retail sales beat at 12:30Z would be the near-term problem.

symbols.why: One point of separation, shorting the weakest currency here against a franc backed by the strongest cyclical data on the board - Swiss GDP +2.3% y/y, manufacturing PMI 57.1, unemployment 3.0% - while Canada's composite contracts at 47.8 and its employment fell 41,700 in August.
symbols.risk: Carry runs hard against it at 2.25% versus 0.00%, and both legs have an event today: the SNB at 07:30Z, where dovish FX language would sell the franc, and Canadian retail sales at 12:30Z. The crude rebound is a CAD tailwind that this position is on the wrong side of.

symbols.why: Flipped from RANGE on the AUD upgrade and the survey divergence in the same session. Britain's composite fell to 51.7, the only major to move the wrong way, with a Budget on October 28 that August's 18.3 billion borrowing print made harder; Australia has the highest cash rate here at 4.35% with about 95% priced for 4.60% on September 29.
symbols.risk: Two red folders point the other way: a September 29 RBA hold, which is TE's own explicit forecast against 95% pricing, and Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow, where any tolerance of above-target inflation would re-rate sterling. Australia's manufacturing survey is contracting at 49.3.

symbols.why: Level for level at 0 each, and the two legs cancel rather than combine. New Zealand offers the steepest projected policy path here and the highest inflation at 4.1%, against unemployment of 5.6% and a currency that is -5.06% on the month; Japan offers 4.7% wage growth and a rising policy rate against softening surveys and an explicit TE hold forecast for October 30. Trade the levels.
symbols.risk: Both tails are live and both are dated: roughly 75% is priced for an RBNZ hike on October 28, and a Ministry of Finance intervention would move the yen leg violently at any moment. Either resolving turns this directional fast.

symbols.why: Both at 0 with offsetting stories. Sterling carries the highest yield on this board at 5.348% and a hawkish MPC minority, against the only major survey that moved the wrong way and an October 28 Budget; the yen carries 4.7% wage growth and a rising policy rate against an explicit TE hold forecast and the widest carry gap in years. Levels, not direction.
symbols.risk: Two red folders inside 36 hours - Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow and the ever-present MoF intervention threat after last Friday's reported rate check - either of which breaks the range. Carry still pays to be long here, which biases the range trade's drift.

symbols.why: Two zero-score currencies whose scores are about to be set by decisions rather than data. Switzerland decides at 07:30Z today with the conditional inflation path and the FX clause as the whole event; Japan's next decision is October 30 with TE explicitly forecasting a hold. Until the SNB speaks this is a levels trade between the two lowest policy rates on the board.
symbols.risk: Ninety minutes to the SNB and an unquantifiable intervention risk on the other leg. A marked-up Swiss conditional path with hawkish FX language plus a quiet yen would break this higher; an MoF operation would break it lower just as fast.

symbols.why: Both upgraded to +1 in the same session, for opposite reasons, so the cross stays flat. The euro's case is a growth surprise - a 53.1 composite and a dated October 29 meeting; the Australian case is a 95%-priced hike to 4.60% in five days against contracting activity at 49.3 manufacturing. Score-for-score there is nothing between them.
symbols.risk: The RBA on September 29 is the resolver, and it is binary against TE's own 4.35% forecast: a hike takes this lower, a hold takes it sharply higher with 95% priced. A euro-area survey that gives back the September jump would do the same from the other side.

symbols.why: Both at 0 and both for the same kind of reason: a hawkish policy path that the domestic economy is struggling to justify. Britain has three of nine voting to hike with a composite PMI falling to 51.7; New Zealand has a projected OCR of 4.00 percent in 2027 with unemployment at 5.6% and rising. Neither side wins on a 4H horizon.
symbols.risk: Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow and the roughly 75% priced for an RBNZ hike on October 28 are the two events that break this, in opposite directions. The kiwi's -5.06% month means positioning is already one-sided.

symbols.why: Both at 0 with genuinely offsetting cases: sterling has the highest yield on this board at 5.348% and a hawkish MPC minority against a softening survey and a Budget; the franc has the strongest cyclical data here - GDP +2.3%, manufacturing PMI 57.1 - against a zero policy rate and a decision ninety minutes away.
symbols.risk: Two red folders in two days, the SNB at 07:30Z today and Bailey at 09:15Z tomorrow. Either could set the direction, and the fiscal risk in the gilt market means sterling's high yield is not a safety feature.

symbols.why: Both at 0 and both carrying policy paths that point up from very different starting points - an OCR at 2.75% with roughly 75% priced for October, against a franc at zero that TE's model keeps flat through 2027. The kiwi's yield advantage is real but it is attached to the weaker economy, with unemployment at 5.6% against Switzerland's 3.0%.
symbols.risk: The SNB at 07:30Z is the immediate risk and the kiwi is already -5.06% on the month, so this pair is short the currency with momentum. A hawkish SNB FX clause would push it lower quickly.

symbols.why: The basket rises when the yen strengthens, and the yen is MIXED at 0, so this is the opposite ticket to the XXX/JPY crosses and it stays neutral with them. The carry gap argues for the basket to fall - USD/JPY touched 158.283 on a 19-year-high US 10-year - while wage growth at 4.7%, a JGB at 3.083 and an armed Ministry of Finance argue it can spike higher without warning.

symbols.why: Flipped from LONG because all three headwinds arrived together and the tailwind reversed. The DAX closed 0.66% lower at 25,410.63 on Wednesday as the Bund 10-year climbed back above 3.5% to 3.5495, the highest since mid-2009; Brent went back through 100 to 102.166 rather than continuing lower; and the euro-area survey jump has put an October 29 ECB hike into the conversation with Nagel already talking about mildly restrictive territory. EU gas at 73.70 is +2.35% on the day.
symbols.risk: The short is fighting the strongest German activity data in a year - a 53.8 composite and 52.9 services, both well above expectations - which is exactly what German equities are supposed to trade on. If the ECB stays quiet and the Saudi pipeline restart pushes Brent back under 100, both headwinds fade and the growth leg wins.

symbols.why: The real-rate leg is now unambiguous. The US 10-year closed at 5.04%, the highest since July 2007, October hike odds moved to about 73%, and DXY is at a two-month high - the three things that cap bullion, all moving at once. Gold at 4,292.75 is -1.12% on the week and -7.84% on the month after Wednesday's 1.2% session decline.

Gold is also the cleanest hedge against the Hormuz tail, and Iran tying any reopening to the US lifting its port blockade means that tail is live - a failed negotiation would take gold back through 4,400 regardless of real rates.

symbols.why: Flipped from LONG, and the leg that broke should be named: the industrial case held and the rates case overwhelmed it. Copper is 6.6942 and +1.64% on the week, so industrial demand did not fail - but silver still fell about 3% on Wednesday to 64.274 and is -6.30% on the month, against gold's -7.84%, as the dollar and a 19-year-high 10-year pulled speculative capital out of the whole complex. Silver's higher beta now works against the position.
symbols.risk: That higher beta cuts both ways and silver turns faster than gold. If the SNB or a soft claims print takes the dollar down, or the Hormuz talks break down, silver outperforms gold on the way back up. This is a momentum short in an instrument that does not respect momentum for long.

symbols.why: Copper is 6.6942 USD/lb on TE, +1.64% on the week and +17.81% on the year, and it held its ground through a session that took both precious metals down - the clearest evidence on this board that the metals selloff was a rates story, not a demand story. It ties directly to the AUD upgrade: the same physical tightness that argues for copper argues for Australia's terms of trade, and TE has the price essentially flat on the month at -0.29% while the dollar rose 2.19%.
symbols.risk: A dollar that keeps making two-month highs is a headwind for every dollar-denominated commodity eventually, and copper is the one with the most direct exposure to Chinese demand, which nothing in this week's data speaks to. The -0.29% month against a +2.19% DXY month means the physical story is already doing work to stand still.

Up: Iran has tied any Hormuz reopening to the US easing military pressure and lifting its port blockade, confirmed transits ran 6.98 million b/d in the week to September 20 against an 18.3 million prewar baseline, and WTI is back to 91.404 with Brent through 100 at 102.166. Down: the Saudi East-West pipeline has restarted after the September 13 drone strike, restoring a route worth about 4 million b/d around the strait.
symbols.risk: Note that a USOIL LONG would normally imply a firm CAD, and CAD is -1 here - that is not an inconsistency but the reason this is RANGE rather than LONG: Canada's weakness is now domestic, with employment down 41,700 and a services PMI at 46.8, so crude alone cannot carry it. Any single headline from the UN General Assembly track can move this 5% in either direction.

catalysts.event: Australia August labour force survey - Australian Bureau of Statistics
catalysts.note: RELEASED at 01:30Z and re-verified on TradingEconomics this morning: Employment Change +39,493 against a 21.5K forecast after July's -15,864, with full-time employment DOWN 6,282, part-time up 45,775, and the unemployment rate at 4.6% from 4.5%, a five-year high, on participation rising to 67.10% from 66.90%. The reason this entry matters more today than it did on release is what did NOT happen: market pricing for the September 29 meeting did not move on it and sits at about 95% for a hike to 4.60%.

catalysts.event: SNB monetary policy assessment and policy rate - Swiss National Bank
catalysts.note: 07:30Z, with 0.00% carried as the ForexFactory consensus, as TE's consensus and as TE's own TEForecast, and the Reuters economist poll unanimous for no change. The rate is not the event. The conditional inflation forecast is: the June assessment published 0.6% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, and Swiss CPI has since doubled to 0.8% in August from 0.4% on energy pass-through, with the June minutes already flagging second-round effects in processed food, transport, tourism and restaurants.

catalysts.event: SNB press conference - Swiss National Bank
catalysts.note: 08:00Z, a separate red folder thirty minutes after the assessment, and the place the FX language is delivered. June's formulation was that 'if necessary, the SNB has an increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market' to counter 'a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc'. That sentence was written for pressure that has since inverted - the franc is 2.84% WEAKER against the dollar on the month - so a reversion to symmetric standby wording is the live outcome and matters more to EUR/CHF and the franc crosses than the rate.

catalysts.event: BoE Governor Bailey speaks - Bank of England
catalysts.note: 09:15Z and now the decisive sterling event of the week, because the September flash survey took away the growth argument for the hawkish minority. Three of nine MPC members voted to hike on September 17 and none voted to cut, with CPI at 3.1% and rising, but the composite PMI has fallen to 51.7 and the gilt 10-year sits at 5.348% five weeks before an October 28 Budget. Explicit tolerance of above-target inflation is the sterling upgrade; acknowledging that the survey changes the November calculus is the downgrade.

catalysts.event: RBA Governor Bullock speaks - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: HAPPENED at 03:10Z Monday, a CEDA fireside chat in Sydney. Its importance has grown rather than faded: reporting has Bullock retiring the RBA's long-standing 'narrow path' framing and saying heat needs to come out of the labour market, and it is the speech that moved the remaining Australian majors onto forecasting a September 29 hike. That pricing survived yesterday's mixed labour force survey intact.

catalysts.event: US September flash PMIs - S&P Global
catalysts.note: HAPPENED at 13:45Z and it is the single biggest input on this page today. Manufacturing 57.0 against a 53.6 forecast and 53.9 previous, the strongest since May 2022; services 58.7 from 56.5; composite 58.4 from 56.0, the highest since July 2021. The survey's price gauges rose to their highest since October 2022 and employment growth ran at a pace not seen since mid-2022 - which is why hike odds and yields moved together.

catalysts.event: Fed Governor Barr and Chicago Fed President Goolsbee speak - Federal Reserve
catalysts.note: HAPPENED. Barr, at a Chicago housing conference: 'In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion', adding that risks to the inflation target have increased while risks to the labour market have receded. Goolsbee: 'This has been nothing like the one-and-done pattern that underpins the case for looking through.' CME FedWatch odds for October 28 moved to about 73% from roughly 55% on Tuesday.

catalysts.event: Euro-area and UK September flash PMIs - S&P Global / HCOB
catalysts.note: HAPPENED and they diverged sharply. The euro-area composite rose to 53.1 from 52.0 against a 51.5 consensus, the fastest in almost three and a half years, with services at 53.0 against 51.7 expected and Germany's composite at 53.8 against 51.8. The UK composite fell to 51.7 from 52.5 with services missing at 51.7 against 52.0. These two prints are the whole basis of today's EUR upgrade and the EUR/GBP long.

catalysts.event: German ifo business climate and ECB Economic Bulletin - ifo Institute / European Central Bank
catalysts.note: Both at 08:00Z, with the ifo forecast at 89.1 from 88.8. After a German flash composite of 53.8 against 51.8 expected, the ifo is the confirmation test: a beat says the survey jump is a turn rather than a spike and strengthens today's EUR upgrade, a miss says the opposite within a day of the call being made.

catalysts.event: Canada July retail sales - Statistics Canada
catalysts.note: 12:30Z, with the headline carried at -0.8% and core at -0.5% against +0.6% and +0.5% previous. This is the nearest test of whether Canada's weakness has moved from its terms of trade into its domestic demand, and it lands on a day when Brent going back above 100 has already repaired the external leg. A beat is the first real argument for taking CAD off -1.

catalysts.event: US initial jobless claims - Department of Labor
catalysts.note: 12:30Z at a 201K forecast from 196K, with continuing claims at 1,730K from 1,769K. With the dollar now long a growth story as well as a rates story, this is the cheapest place for that story to be tested: a print above 215K would be the first labour-market evidence against a Fed that has just told the market risks have shifted away from employment.

catalysts.event: Fed speakers Williams, Barkin, Hammack and Paulson - Federal Reserve
catalysts.note: Williams 08:10Z, Barkin 12:30Z, Hammack 12:50Z, Paulson 14:10Z - four in one session, the day after Barr and Goolsbee moved October odds to about 73%. Williams is the one that matters most: as Vice Chair of the FOMC he rarely leads pricing but confirms it, and an endorsement of Barr's framing would make the October hike close to settled.

catalysts.event: BoE speakers Dhingra, Breeden and Lombardelli - Bank of England
catalysts.note: Dhingra 09:30Z, Breeden 13:30Z, Lombardelli 14:00Z - three MPC members in one session, the day after the UK survey missed and the day before Bailey. Dhingra has been the committee's most dovish voice; the interesting signal would be any of the three acknowledging that a composite PMI at 51.7 changes what November can be.

catalysts.event: Japan BoJ core CPI - Bank of Japan
catalysts.note: 05:00Z at a 1.5% forecast from 1.6%. The Bank's own preferred measure, and it lands with TE explicitly forecasting a hold at 1.25% on October 30. catalysts.event: US durable goods orders and revised UoM sentiment - Census Bureau / University of Michigan
catalysts.note: Durable goods 12:30Z with the headline -0.3% forecast from +1.1% and core +0.6% from +0.4%; revised UoM sentiment 14:00Z at 47.4 from 47.8 with inflation expectations previously 4.6%. catalysts.event: RBA interest rate decision - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: 04:30Z, and the largest single disagreement between market pricing and the canonical source on this board. TE has now attached an explicit TEForecast of 4.35% to this row - a dated hold - while market pricing sits at about 95% for a hike to 4.60% and all four Australian majors forecast it. Meeting Minutes follow October 13. With that much priced, the asymmetry is entirely on a hold, and it is the stated invalidation of today's AUD upgrade.

catalysts.event: BoJ Summary of Opinions from the September meeting - Bank of Japan
catalysts.note: 23:50Z and the nearest scheduled insight into a 7-2 vote that took the policy rate to its highest since April 1995. With TE's model carrying 1.75 percent in 2027 - 50bp above spot - and wage growth at 4.7%, the question is whether the two dissenters wanted more or less, and whether the majority framed 1.25% as a stopping point or a waypoint.

catalysts.event: ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts - European Central Bank
catalysts.note: 11:30Z, and the only ECB item TE's calendar carries between now and the end of the year. It is the first chance to see whether Nagel's 'mildly restrictive' language reflects a wider shift inside the Council or an individual view, and it now reads into a dated October 29 meeting rather than into an undated void.

catalysts.event: BoC Business Outlook Survey and Survey of Consumer Expectations - Bank of Canada
catalysts.note: 14:30Z and the nearer of the two Canadian inputs before the October 28 decision. After employment fell 41,700 and with the services PMI at 46.8, this survey is where the Bank finds out whether firms are responding to the energy shock by raising prices or by cutting demand - the exact distinction Macklem's 'we will not let their effects broaden' conditional turns on.

catalysts.note: Three events on one date and they interact. The Fed decides at 18:00Z with about 73% priced for a move to 4.25%; the Bank of Canada decides at 13:45Z alongside its Monetary Policy Report with no TE forecast attached; and the UK Budget lands against borrowing already 8.1 billion above the OBR profile. The USD/CAD long and the sterling reads both resolve on this date.

catalysts.event: UN General Assembly, Hormuz status and the Saudi East-West pipeline restart

Iran has floated reopening the strait within seven days if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, and Trump has described a three-hour meeting with an Iranian delegation as having gone very well - while Iran publicly called his UN threats a sign of 'strategic desperation'. Against that, Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline has restarted after the September 13 drone attack, restoring a route worth about 4 million b/d around the strait.

catalysts.note: Undated by nature and closer than it was. USD/JPY touched 158.283 yesterday on the US yield surge, a rate check was reported late last Friday into holiday liquidity, and the August coordinated operation with the US Treasury was explicitly described by both sides as repeatable. Tokyo is back from three days of holiday, which removes the thin-liquidity cover that has been the usual precondition.

geopolitics: The de-escalation trade that drove this page for a week has stalled, and the reversal is the most important market fact of the last twenty-four hours after the US PMI. Start with the prices, all from TradingEconomics this morning. WTI is 91.404, having been 89.263 yesterday, and Brent has gone back through the round number to 102.166; the daily readings are -0.82% and -0.89% respectively, which tells you the rebound happened in Wednesday's session and is holding rather than extending. On the week both are still lower - WTI -10.31%, Brent -2.53% - but the monthly numbers are what the risk premium actually looks like: WTI +10.98% and Brent +17.07%. Gas turned with it: EU gas is 73.70 and +2.35% on the day, UK gas 183.90 and +2.46%, with German gas the one exception at 72.85 and -1.70%. Now the two pieces of news underneath, because they point in opposite directions and both are real. Bearish: Saudi Arabia has restarted its East-West pipeline, shut since September 13 after drone attacks halted crude loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu. That line normally moves about 4 million barrels a day, roughly 4% of global supply, entirely around the Strait of Hormuz, and reporting has flows running at a reduced rate immediately after the restart with Yanbu exports resuming this week. Bullish: Tehran has put a price on the strait. Iran has indicated it would reopen Hormuz within seven days if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports - a conditional reopening, not a reopening - and at the same time called Trump's General Assembly threats a sign of 'strategic desperation', while Trump described a three-hour meeting between an administration official and an Iranian delegation as having gone very well. The physical baseline says how far there is to go: confirmed transits averaged 6.98 million barrels a day in the seven days to September 20, about 38% of the 18.3 million prewar level, against an IEA characterisation of this as the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. The FX read has changed in three specific places. First, Australia. Yesterday's AUD downgrade was explicitly conditioned on crude extending lower, and it did not - which removes the second leg of that downgrade and is half the reason AUD returns to +1 with a 95%-priced hike five days away. Second, Canada. Macklem's hawkish conditional was written at US$100 oil, and Brent is back through it even though WTI is not, so the external case for the loonie has genuinely repaired; CAD stays at -1 only because its problem has migrated inward, to employment down 41,700 and the only contracting PMIs on this board. Third, Germany. The GER40 long carried here is closed and flipped short, because falling Brent was the tailwind and it has gone, while the Bund 10-year at 3.5495 is the highest since mid-2009 and EU gas is rising again. The franc and gold, the two haven expressions, are both notably NOT participating - USD/CHF at 0.82421 has the franc 2.84% weaker on the month and gold is -7.84% on the month - which says the market is treating this as an energy supply event being negotiated rather than a security event being escalated. That is the assumption to watch: it is the one that fails fastest if the UN track breaks down.
